projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with Edward Bishop by Diane Salmon [November 22, 2002]

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Today is Friday, November 22, 2002, and this is the beginning of an interview with Edward C. Bishop at his home at 1748 Rolling Ridge Lane in Toms River, New Jersey. Mr. Bishop is 87 years old, having been born on March 17, 1915. My name is Diane Salmon. Edward Bishop is my uncle. He is my mother's brother.
Uncle Eddie, could you state for the recording, what were the war or wars and branch of service you served in?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: World War II and Korea, U.S.Navy.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: And what was your rank?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: My final rank was Commander.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: And in what theaters did you serve?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Pacific, Atlantic, and Mediterranean.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: How did you happen to become a naval officer in WWII?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: In the summer of 1941 I broke my ankle playing softball with the Seaside Heights Beach Patrol. This enabled me to return to my teaching and coaching position at Bellport, New York High School for another school year and granted me time to seek out and decide what type of military service I would perform.

I searched out various options and concluded I would like to be a naval aviator. After going through all the procedures I was directed to report to the 3rd Naval District to be sworn in. I reported promptly at 8 a.m. and was told to stand by and that Commander so-and-so would swear me in. At 1 p.m. after no one showed up, I decided that if that was the way I would be treated before I went in, how would I be treated after I was in? So I left.

Shortly thereafter several of my fellow coaches in Suffolk County, New York had entered what was called the Tunney Fish program- they entered this program as Chief Petty Officers. Since I had been coaching and deeply involved in physical education activities, I applied for and was accepted in the program headed by Gene Tunney, the heavyweight boxing champion. Once again I was to be sworn in at the 3rd Naval District. Walking down the corridor at 3rd Naval District Headquarters, a LT JG came from the opposite direction and asked what I was doing there. After I told him, he said " Ed, you don't want to do that" and I asked him what I did want to do and he said, "come with me". That day I went through all the tests and interviews and walked out an Ensign in the Reserve with orders to a new Communications Officers School being set up at Cornell University.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: What kind of training did you receive in communication officers' school and where did you train

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: My orders said specifically not to report in at Cornell until 1 July 1942. I arrived at Cornell on June 30, 1942, and did not report in until 1 July. Later, to my dismay, I learned that half the class had reported on 30 June so they were later eligible for earlier promotions based on being on active duty on 30 June!

After several months at Cornell, my class was moved to a new Officers Communications School at Harvard. Several other officers and I served as the nucleus of platoon leaders and athletic team members. Upon my graduation I was to report to DD476 Hutchins. 476 was one of the destroyers designated by President Roosevelt to have an observation seaplane aboard as an experiment. A determination was made not to have the aircraft on board and a second torpedo mount of five tubes was installed in the States.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Were you one of the plank owners on the Hutchins?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: No, unfortunately I wasn't. Several days before the Hutchins was commissioned on 17 November 1942, I visited the ship, which was in the Boston Navy Yard. Upon return to school at Harvard I requested permission to attend the commissioning ceremony on 17 November. I was asked if I had been invited; I responded that I had not. The reply was "no" even though I would be aboard for several years!

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: That's really unfortunate. Where did the ship go for shakedown training?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Shakedown training was in Casco Bay in Maine and in Guantanamo, Cuba.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: And then I understand you made a trip to Galveston, Texas?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, what we did after shakedown training we began our trip to the Pacific. We escorted two tankers to Galveston, Texas. Tom Graham, executive officer, and I were almost shot at the Blossom Heath, a nightclub outside Houston as we waited for the owner to drive us back to our hotel in Houston.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: That would have been a short war! Where did you go after Houston?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: We headed to the Pacific traveling through the Panama Canal and arrived in San Diego. We left San Diego escorting two tankers to New Caledonia and Espirito Santo. While there one of our 5"38 guns was removed and put aboard the destroyer Nicholas, to replace one of theirs that had burned out. Shortly after arriving back in Pearl Harbor our gun was replaced. While testing the new gun the firing cam did not function properly and the gun was fired into our forward. The net result: 13 of our shipmates were killed.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Did you go on to Alaska at one point?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: After returning to San Diego, we headed with a LST group for Adak, Alaska at the end of the Aleutians. On 15 August we took part in the occupation of Kiska, only to find that the Japanese had already left. We then took a trip out into the Bering Straits around the Pribilofs. Russ Ennis, the ship's doctor, loved fishing and had tried to catch a fish at every place we had stopped. At Kiska, he put two hooks on his line- it no sooner had hit the water than two huge fish grabbed the bait. As he tried to pull them in, his line parted and he landed nothing!

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Did your ship see any action after you left the Aleutians?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, we left the Aleutians later in November 1943 headed for Pearl Harbor and then New Guinea. Shortly after arriving in Milne Bay we left for Cape Gloucester, screening LSTs for the landing there. We were leading a column of DDs. The Brownson was 300 yards astern of us. A Japanese aircraft put a 500-pound bomb right down her stack- both bow and stern came up and the ship sank immediately. Unfortunately, the Bronson was staffed with a green crew and had not set their depth charges on "safe". As a result the charges exploded as they went down into the water and killed many of the sailors who had been fortunate enough to get into the water.

At the same time one of our DDs shot down a U.S. P-38 aircraft, a very distinctive twin tail boomed aircraft. The pilot later visited the Captain of the ship and had a brief discussion concerning proper protocol.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: I can only imagine! Wasn't your ship damaged in New Guinea?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, shortly after, the Hutchins was escorting LSTs to a landing in Saidor, it collided with DD Smith and was sent to Cairns, Australia, to have our bow repaired.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Where did you sail after the ship was repaired?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: In late February 1944, the Hutchins was part of an amphibious group under the command of Admiral Crutchley of the Royal Australian Navy that assumed control over the Admiralty Islands. During the New Guinea campaign and the landings in the Philippines, HMAS destroyers Arunta and Warramunga were assigned to our squadron Desron 24. There was also an Australian cruiser HMAS Shropshire (affectionately called the Slop Shoot) that joined our campaigns throughout the conquest of New Guinea. It was very convenient to share the hospitality of Australian ships tied alongside, especially at their happy hour.

One incident stands out for me with the Admiralties. General MacArthur went ashore there. When he returned to his ship they called for someone to pick up the briefcase of "Private Smith" which had been left behind. Even though he was in full military regalia, Private Smith was General MacArthur.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Offhand how would you say the Australian Navy compared with the U.S.Navy?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: They fitted in very well in our squadron and performed admirably, especially the Arunta which made torpedo runs during the Battle of Surigao Straits in the same division that the Hutchins was.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: I understand that the Hutchins also served in the Admiralty Islands. Did your ship see action there?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, the control that I mentioned and General MacArthur's visit ashore were related to our invasion of the Admiralties. Somewhere along the line the Hutchins had the "ready duty" in the Admiralties. That's when a ship is ready to get underway when all other ships are at anchor. The purpose was to be able to get underway as soon a possible. We received notice to get underway to rescue a downed pilot. We did get underway and traveled quite a distance when we were told the downed pilot had been picked up by a submarine. I believe that pilot was President George Bush.

Another rescue of aircraft personnel took place a short time later. One of the B-24's flying out of the Admiralties was shot down about 180 miles south of Truk. We were directed to pick up the three survivors of that aircraft mishap. Unfortunately, or rather fortunately, our whaleboat picked up the three aviation people and I was not required to swim out to be of assistance.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: I understand you did a surprise bombardment of Wewak in New Guinea?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, in May we made a surprise bombardment sweep with several other DDs of Wewak. Wewak was almost 200 miles behind enemy lines. Amazingly we thought the Japs could not hit us- or- if they did sink us, someone would pick us up very shortly. In June we participated in shore bombardment of Wadke and Biak. Five Japanese destroyers approached as we were conducting the bombardment. They released their troop-laden barges and began retiring. They were pursued by the Hutchins and retired rapidly. The squadron commander ordered the Hutchins to break off the pursuit but Captain Cal Laning of the Hutchins preferred to continue the pursuit long after he was ordered to return.

The Hutchins was hit by a large shell during the shore bombardment of Biak. Charlie Matulas was in charge of the damage control party on the main deck. A shell passed Charley by a few feet, traveled through the ship and exploded on the other side. Charley was aghast when he observed large pools of red material on the deck and feared someone had been hit. It proved out that the shell had passed through a foodlocker and in the process and hit a bottle of ketchup!

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: In July did you do anything?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, shortly after that we were granted R & R in Sydney, Australia. On entry to Sydney harbor our signalmen were extremely busy. It seems signals were handled by women in the Australian Navy. My guys were making dates for when they arrived. They were shocked when I commented on it later —they didn't realize that I could read the code.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: If I recall correctly, it was after this time that your ship was involved in the famous Battle of Leyte Gulf?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: We arrived on 20 October 1944 for the landings at Leyte Gulf. We had been held over from returning to the States in order to make the invasion and then later to do battle. On entry into the Gulf, Captain Laning was playing his accordion to salve the anxieties of those of us on the bridge. The area we had fire support was Red Beach, where the Tacloban airstrip is, where General MacArthur waded ashore. Perhaps the most memorable sight during the fire support/bombardment amphibious landing was seeing a canoe approach the ship with two Filipinos in the bow proudly holding up an American flag!

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: I understand the Hutchins was extremely involved in the action in the Surigao Straits?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, we were. That was the greatest naval battle in history. Six or seven days after we made the invasion of Tacloban, we learned that the Japanese fleet was coming out from three different locations. One of which was the Surigao Straits. The Hutchins, Daly, and Australian destroyer Arunta formed one group of destroyers on the starboard side as we went down into the Straits. Three other cans were on the port side. There were also two other divisions of destroyers that came later.

We closed on the Jap line attempting to get into Leyte Gulf, fired 5 torpedoes and much of our 5'38 ammo, and retired to the starboard side near the land hoping the Japs could not track us. We then made a second run on the oncoming Japs, fired our last five torpedoes and almost all of the rest of our 5"38 guns.

Scared? Hell yes, but we had trained in this type of action so many times that it went smoothly. Hutchins was credited with helping to sink two cruisers and one destroyer. We were directed to pick up Jap sailors in the water for interrogation. They refused but complied after the encouragement of a few 20mm shots over their heads.

A sad note: the USS Grant was in the port side column. They were told to steer to port after their contact with the Jap line. Unfortunately they turned to starboard and were mistaken as a ship of the Jap line and were shelled badly by the American Big Boys (Battleships) who were about to cross the T. In all the publicity about the six BBs that survived and were rebuilt after at Pearl Harbor, the BBs seem to be credited for victory at Surigao. We destroyer men know that the tin cans deserve most of the credit. During the accident with the Grant, 38 sailors were killed and four wounded, almost one third of the ship's complement.

After Surigao, the Hutchins returned back to the United States. After arrival at the dock, an award ceremony was held. I was awarded a Bronze Star with valor for my work in the combat information center during the invasion and after the battle.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: When did you leave the Hutchins?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Shortly after our arrival in the United States, I received my orders for transfer off the Hutchins. I had expected to receive orders to Pacific Fleet Training Center since I had written several articles about training radiomen at sea aboard destroyers. Instead I was transferred to the pre-commissioning detail of a new class of DDs, the Gearing DD-710, the 2200 ton long hull. Ninety-nine others in the Gearing class were made. During the 1960's, the Gearing was one of the key destroyers to turn back the Russians from Cuba. I was not disappointed with my assignment to the Gearing because the ship was being built at the Federal Shipyard Kearny/Newark about ten miles from my home in Wood-Ridge, New Jersey. I was asked to recommend changes in their C.I.C. and many of my suggestions were adopted for the Gearing and future Gearing class destroyers.

The Gearing was commissioned at the Brooklyn Navy Yard on 3 May 1945. I was very proud to be able to invite my family to attend the ceremony, as well as an old salt, the Chief of Police, and the mayor of my hometown.

Shortly after the commissioning we spent a month or so in Cuba undergoing shakedown training. When we returned to the Brooklyn Navy Yard in late June 1945, I was bringing the ship alongside a pier. The line handling crew was very slow and I was concerned we would move away from the dock. In a loud fashion I urged the line handlers to move a little faster. Shortly after we moored my Uncle came aboard. He was a shipyard worker and had been one of the line handlers!

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: After the shakedown cruise where did the Gearing go?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Our next duty station was Norfolk. On 15 August 1945 the war with Japan was ended—to the jubilation of every ship in the harbor—every bell, whistle, and other noisemaker went on and on through the night.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: From Norfolk we were assigned to Casco Bay, Maine, for a couple of months—;conducted a memorial service at sea there and then on to New London for Navy Day. Then back to Norfolk and later to Pensacola to serve as plane guard for the Guadalcanal CVE 60, training new pilots. On the base at Pensacola they had a plane and a dummy pilot memorial between the Officers Club and the pier where Gearing was moored. There was many a toast to the fallen pilot in the wee hours of the morning.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: When did you leave the Gearing?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: I stood my last watch aboard the Gearing on 11 December 1945. I was detached from the ship with orders to report to the nearest Naval District for discharge. I knew the orders meant the 3rd Naval District in New York (since I lived in New Jersey) but interpreted them to mean the 6th Naval District in nearby New Orleans. (They explained where I should have gone- after two weeks of fun in New Orleans!)

At the 3rd Naval District I was offered a spot promotion to LCDR and assignment to a destroyer as executive offer. I declined, remembering the reservists on extended active duty were the first to be released involuntarily after WWII.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: What did you do after you left active duty?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: At my separation they were pushing going to work for the VA, which was expanding rapidly. I decided to try it since my replacement in the Bellport School System was mid-year and I didn't want him to have to lose his job. Plus I didn't want to deal with teenagers so soon after going through my duties in the Navy. I continued work for the VA until recalled for Korea in 1950.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: What did you do in 1948 and 1949?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: I was working for the Veterans Administration.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Were you involved in any naval activities also?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, sometime around 1948 or 1949 I decided to become active in Navy affairs and joined with Surface Battalion 3-37 in my hometown in a non-pay billet. In mid 1950 my commanding officer asked if I wanted a pay billet. I accepted and three weeks later had orders to active duty since all officers in pay billet had been activated. My orders were to Comdesron 22, Commander Destroyer Squadron 22, as operations officer but wound up as operations officer of Desdiv 222, Destroyer Division 222, when I found it necessary to delay my entry into active duty.

The Squadron Commander was engaged in bringing four destroyers back to active commission in Charleston, S.C. As a result, without much work to do, we spent much time at the golf course on the base, etc. I recently visited the decommissioned Charleston Navy Yard and could only find one hole of the old golf course and it was covered with 1 1/2 to 2 feet of grass.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: You went to the Mediterranean after that didn't you?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, Destroyer Squadron 22 participated in a Mediterranean cruise from September 15, 1951 to February of 1942. Prior to departure to the Med the Commodore had directed that all destroyers top off their fuel to insure it would be unnecessary to refuel before reaching the Med. One of the destroyers did not refuel to top capacity and ran out of fuel prior to reaching Gibraltar. After our arrival in the Mediterranean Ault, the flagship of Desdiv 222, visited Lisbon, Portugal. One of my most favorable memories was the bullfight that another officer and I attended with 2 Portuguese gentlemen we met in a club there.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: You went to a lot of interesting places in Europe. Did you get to do much sightseeing?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, the cruise was worth 25 or 30 thousand dollars! We would depart one of the many ports in the Mediterranean, go out to sea, conduct training exercises for a week or so, and then visit another port for a week or two. Usually I arranged the visits with local officials. The Commodore would take me with him for early walks in the particular places of interest in the town/city of the country where we were. I saw many catacombs. We even had an audience with Pope Pius XII. I especially remember the visit of orphans to the ship in Golfe Juan in France on Christmas. I also remember a taxi falling off the pier into the water after bringing sailors back to the ship from liberty in Kavalla, Greece. I recall a reception for a Greek general who had just returned from Korea. I also remember clearly my discussions with a Greek metropolitan at that reception even though he couldn't speak English and I couldn't speak a word of Greek.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: There were many other experiences in the Mediterranean that we couldn't include in the audiotape because of the time restraint, but for the benefit of Commander Bishop's family, some of them are listed here.

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: * met Bill Sherwood, my protégé from the Hutchins and Morty Andrewsen, engineer of the Hutchins, who was serving as chief engineer of a carrier
* Russian claims we had established a naval base at Naples
* horse chariot races on the streets of Palermo * entertainment at British Consulate in Cyprus
* visiting Trieste, which had not yet been returned to Italy
* tour of the new Italian cruise liner Guilio Caesari on its maiden voyage
* working with Greek and Italian naval vessels
* being offered the goat's eye as a treat at a Greek cocktail party
* the French and Italian Rivieras
* being approached by a "typical" French person on the Ville Franche, France who wanted to exchange currency. He turned out to be one of my employees at the VA!

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: I understand you came back from the Mediterranean in February 1952. How was the trip back?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: You asked a difficult question. The trip back was rough, rough, rough. The Ault, which was Condesdiv 222's flagship, rolled 55 degrees, ruptured a steam line, and had to put into Bermuda to take on fuel. We were lucky to get back to the States.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Did you stay involved with the Navy even after you left active duty?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: After my release from active duty in 1952 I joined a Bureau of Ships (Buships) Reserve Unit in New York and continued with that until I was retired after 26 years in the active Navy Reserve. I did also serve as a member of the Secretary of the Navy's Advisory Committee on Retired Affairs for 5 years, and for 10 years as a member of the Blue and Gold recruiting team (public info and recruiters of the Naval Academy.

I had the opportunity to have some great 2-week training periods. I attended the Naval War College, the National War College, Industrial College of the Armed Forces, Strategy and Tactics of Communism, and - oh yes- a trip aboard a destroyer to Bermuda.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Do you hear from any of the men you served with in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Yes, I was retired in 1968 and another one of the officers and I met at a Tin Can Sailors meeting some 15 years ago and decided we should try to locate the sailors from the Hutchins. We were successful. We set up an organization for the Hutchins and I served as its President for four years and we have held reunions for the past 14 years. I also helped to develop an organization for retirees of the Gearing and served on its Board of Trustees for a few years.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: I have two final questions. How did your service and experiences affect your life?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: The Navy became part of my life- a great part of my life- in 1942. I have pictures at home when I was 5 years old in a sailor suit, so my relationship with sailors and naval matters has gone from those days. I'm still very active and interested with what happens with our guys and gals in the service.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Is there anything you'd like to add that we haven't covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: Well, for someone that's thinking of the Navy, or going into the Navy, think of it as place that you can develop yourself-there are all kinds of education and jobs- that you can make yourself into almost anything you choose. There are wide opportunities and all you have to do step in and work at it.

sp.speaker: Diane Salmon
sp.p: Thank you very much for sharing your recollections and thank you for your service to the United States of America in the U.S. Navy.

sp.speaker: Edward C. Bishop
sp.p: I'm very proud that I've done so.
